title: Rabbi Yoshia bar Gizora
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: English translation and editorial notes prepared for Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He is mentioned at the beginning of [Yerushalmi Shabbat, chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.3.1.4), as serving Rabbi Zeira. At the beginning of [Taanit, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.1.3), Rabbi Yona says that Yeshua bar Gezora and Rabbi Zeira disagreed. At the beginning of [Midrash Shmuel](https://www.sefaria.org/Midrash_Shmuel.1.1), Rabbi Yona reports in Rabbi Yehoshua bar Gezora’s name: “All silences are bad,” etc.[^1] This saying comes from the end of [Yerushalmi Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.9.5.19), where the attribution is Rabbi Yona in the name of Rabbi Yosi bar Gezra. Perhaps the name had been abbreviated ר״י and was turned into Rabbi Yosi, whereas it should in fact read Rabbi Yehoshua.[^2]

notes.text: Hyman’s printed page 652 has כרביא, with resh; the Hebrew transcription has כדביא, with dalet. The Krakow 1893 Midrash Shmuel 1:1 also has כרביא. “Silences” follows Ohr LaYesharim on Yerushalmi Berakhot 9:5:19, which records both orders of “good” and “bad” in the Midrash’s textual tradition. Hyman has ordinary instances as bad and those concerning Torah as good. The Guggenheimer Yerushalmi has כדבייא and the opposite order; Penei Moshe proposes reversing it and understands the word as lying.

רפ״ג and רפ״ד mean the beginning of chapters 3 and 4. The sources vary between Yoshia, Yeshua and Yehoshua, and between Gizora, Gezora, Gezura and Gezra; Hyman’s printed Berakhot attribution has Gezora, while the Guggenheimer text has Yosi ben Gezira. ר״י is retained because Hyman is discussing that abbreviation. His initial “perhaps” and final “should in fact read” express different degrees of confidence in his proposed textual history.
